name: Demosaicing Pattern Residual
description: Analyzes demosaicing interpolation residuals — real camera images contain CFA demosaicing patterns absent in AI-generated content (Swaminathan et al., 2008).
mechanism:
This method exploits the fact that real camera images undergo color filter array (CFA) demosaicing, leaving periodic interpolation artifacts that AI-generated images lack:

1. **CFA Pattern Estimation**: Most digital cameras use a Bayer CFA where each pixel captures only one color channel (RGGB). The missing two channels are reconstructed via demosaicing interpolation. The method estimates which CFA pattern was used by testing all four Bayer phase offsets and selecting the one that produces the most periodic residual in the Fourier domain.

2. **Interpolation Residual Extraction**: For the estimated CFA, the method re-interpolates the image using bilinear demosaicing and subtracts the original, yielding the demosaicing residual. In authentic photos, this residual exhibits strong periodic components at specific frequencies (e.g., peaks at (π, π) and (0, π) in the 2D DFT for Bayer patterns), reflecting the underlying sampling grid.

3. **Periodicity Strength Measurement**: The method computes the peak-to-average ratio (PAR) of the residual's power spectrum at the expected CFA frequencies. Authentic images typically show PAR > 5 dB, while AI-generated images show PAR < 1 dB, as they lack any CFA sampling structure.

4. **Tampering Localization**: For forgery detection, the analysis is performed on overlapping 64×64 blocks. Blocks where the CFA pattern is absent or inconsistent with the dominant pattern are flagged as potentially manipulated or AI-generated. The method outputs a tampering probability map based on the local PAR values.
parameters:
Block size: 64×64 pixels for local analysis
CFA patterns tested: 4 Bayer phase offsets
PAR threshold: 3 dB (authentic vs. AI boundary)
Re-interpolation method: bilinear demosaicing
Frequency peaks: (π, π), (0, π), (π, 0)
Minimum image size: 128×128 pixels
accuracy: 85–93% detection accuracy for distinguishing real camera images from AI-generated content. CFA detection accuracy reaches 97% on raw or lightly processed images. JPEG compression reduces accuracy to 78% at quality factor 75. Tampering localization F1-score of 0.82 on standard forgery benchmarks.
source: Swaminathan, A., Wu, M., & Liu, K. J. R. (2008). Digital Image Forensics via Intrinsic Fingerprints. IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, 3(1), 101–117.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated images by verifying the absence of CFA demosaicing artifacts. Localizing spliced or inpainted regions where demosaicing patterns are missing or inconsistent. Camera model identification based on the specific demosaicing algorithm used (bilinear, VNG, AHD, etc.).
strengths:
• Exploits a fundamental difference between camera-captured and AI-generated images
• High accuracy on raw and lightly processed photographs
• Provides pixel-level tampering localization
• CFA pattern is inherent to the imaging hardware and difficult to forge
• Can identify specific camera models based on their demosaicing algorithm
limitations:
• Heavy JPEG compression or resizing can destroy CFA periodicity
• Images from Foveon (X3) sensors or multi-shot cameras lack standard CFA patterns
• Some post-processing tools (Photoshop, Lightroom) may partially suppress CFA artifacts
• Advanced AI models trained on camera-processed images may learn to approximate CFA patterns
• Requires minimum 128×128 pixel regions for reliable frequency analysis
